newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - China mutual funds lag stocks, bonds.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - China mutual funds lag stocks, bonds.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Shanghai teachers thought they had hit the jackpot when they invested in a mutual fund run by one of China's top brokerages.

The Baoding Fund has outperformed all other funds in China, growing 85 percent since it started in January 1994 -- but the teachers are unhappy because the fund has not been listed on the stock exchange as they had hoped.

The teachers, like millions of other Chinese, bought into the fund in the early 1990s when the stock markets in Shanghai and Shenzhen were booming and it appeared as if listings were just around the corner.

The funds were set up to channel money from individuals into stocks, real estate and industrial projects. Those that did get approval for listings realised huge profits, but the authorities have not approved any for listing since mid-1993.

The problem is that regulation of mutual funds has lagged behind that of stocks and treasury bills, China's two most popular trading instruments, while Beijing works out what kind of fund industry it wants.

"The teachers are pressing us because they want it to be listed," said Shao Jiejun, assistant to the president of the Fund Management Department of Shenyin & Wanguo Securities which manages the closed-end 10-year Baoding Fund.
"If it were listed, it could reach at least five times its face value of one yuan," he said.

Baoding is one of about 70 mutual funds in China, with assets totalling 10 billion yuan ($1.2 billion), but only 22 are listed on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges, making them the poor relations on the block.
In the first eight months of 1996, trading of the 22 listed funds amounted to 27.7 billion yuan compared with total stock trading of 382.525 billion yuan.
The Baoding Fund was worth 184.5 million yuan on August 31, up from its initial 100 million, invested by 90,000 people in 1993, most of them primary and middle school teachers.

The teachers cannot trade their units until they are listed and cannot recover their money until the fund reaches maturity in 2004. Since it was launched they have a dividend payment of 0.185 yuan per unit of one yuan.

Despite three years of discussions, the central bank has not published regulations governing the listing and trading of mutual funds. In the meantime, holders of unlisted closed-end funds cannot trade them or sell them back to the fund managers.

Central bank deputy governor Yin Jieyan said last week that regulations on securities investment funds and Sino-foreign investment funds were in the final stage of discussion and would be promulgated in foreseeable future.
He said the scale of the mutual funds was small and their operations not standardised and China needed to learn from the experience of such funds in advanced and developing countries.

One fund manager said the main reason for the delay in publishing the regulations was disagreement over who in Beijing should have authority over them, the central bank or the Securities Commission under the State Council (cabinet).

Pu Zengping, a lawyer with the Shanghai Fanya Law Office, said that managers of some funds mixed their own money with money entrusted to them and that many funds had lost money in real estate investments, although such losses had not appeared on their balance sheets.
He called for clear guidelines on the responsibilities of fund managers and controls on the use of funds, especially in high-risk investments.

An official newspaper last weekend said a mutual fund with assets of 120 million yuan had been wound up by its operator and its assets returned to investors because it failed to reach expected profit levels in the first case of its kind in China.

The biggest known loss was by Shenyang Fumin, a fund listed on the Shanghai stock exchange, which lent 17 million yuan for two years to a real estate company in Dalian in 1992 but has not received a cent in return.
In April 1996, it won a judgement in a provincial court against the Dalian firm for repayment of principle and interest but the Dalian company has appealed against the decision.
